title.text: Exploring and visualising data with Python: from a new file to a finding

objects.text: How do I explore an unfamiliar dataset in one sitting and find what is worth reporting?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 11 of 24  |  Module C: Analyse and explain
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Last session you asked a database questions in SQL. Today you meet a file you have never seen, which is where most analysts start. You will learn the routine for your first hour with a new file, you will draw charts with matplotlib and seaborn, and you will meet a result that fools almost everyone the first time.

By the end you will have a notebook with eight charts and three findings.

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can run the same exploratory data analysis routine on any new file, in the same order. You can draw five kinds of chart with matplotlib and seaborn and say which one fits which question. And you can tell a count from a rate, spot a seasonal pattern, and write a finding that states a number, a comparison and a limit.

The charts come from the Lakeside Mart orders, and you will draw your own in the lab.

We have two hours. The first ten minutes bring back SQL from Session 10 and set the question for today. Then forty-five minutes of concepts with laptops closed, so you can watch the charts and follow the reasoning. After a ten minute break you open the notebook in Google Colab for a forty-five minute lab: predict, run, read and change.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  In SQL, what is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
2.  Why did you check each SQL result against pandas?
3.  Which SQL clause turns many order lines into one number per branch?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 10. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. In SQL, what is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?

A good answer is this. WHERE keeps rows before the grouping. HAVING keeps groups after the aggregation, such as a count or a sum.

Question two. Why did you check each SQL result against pandas?

A good answer is this. Two different routes to the same number is the best evidence that the number is right.

Question three. Which SQL clause turns many order lines into one number per branch?

A good answer is this. GROUP BY, together with an aggregate function such as COUNT or SUM.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 10

rows.text: In SQL, what is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
WHERE keeps rows before the grouping. HAVING keeps groups after the aggregation, such as a count or a sum.
Why did you check each SQL result against pandas?
Two different routes to the same number is the best evidence that the number is right.
Which SQL clause turns many order lines into one number per branch?
GROUP BY, together with an aggregate function such as COUNT or SUM.

slides.notes:
Here are the answers to the three warm-up questions. WHERE keeps rows before any grouping happens, and HAVING keeps groups after the aggregation, so a branch with more than a thousand orders is a HAVING. You checked each SQL result against pandas because two different routes to the same number is the best evidence that the number is right.

We use that habit again today, because a chart can look convincing when the numbers behind it are wrong. And GROUP BY with an aggregate function such as COUNT or SUM turns many order lines into one number per branch. Which of the three did you find hardest?

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A repeatable routine of looks, summaries and charts that you run on a new dataset before you model it or report on it.
The Figure is the whole page. The Axes is the plot area on that page where the data are drawn and labelled.
A count is how many. A rate divides the count by what could have happened, such as returns per 100 lines sold.
A pattern that comes back at the same time every year, such as a December peak.
One sentence that states a number, a comparison and a limit.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Exploratory data analysis (EDA). A repeatable routine of looks, summaries and charts that you run on a new dataset before you model it or report on it.

Figure and Axes (matplotlib). The Figure is the whole page. The Axes is the plot area on that page where the data are drawn and labelled.

Count and rate. A count is how many. A rate divides the count by what could have happened, such as returns per 100 lines sold.

Seasonality (with trend and noise). A pattern that comes back at the same time every year, such as a December peak.

Finding. One sentence that states a number, a comparison and a limit.

title.text:
Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is a six-step
routine you repeat on every new file

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_ad286d96.png
objects.alt: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is a six-step routine you repeat on every new file

objects.text: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is what you do in Excel when you scroll, filter and pivot a new sheet. Python lets you write the routine down so it runs the same way every time.

slides.notes:
When you meet a new file, you do not start with a model or a report. You explore it. The name is exploratory data analysis, or EDA. In Excel you do it by scrolling, filtering and building a quick pivot table. In Python we write the routine down.

Step one is to look: the shape, the data types and the missing values. Step two is to summarise each numeric variable. Step three is to draw one variable at a time, and step four to draw two together. Step five is to compare groups with counts and rates.

Step six is to write a finding. If you cannot write the sentence, you have not finished exploring. Which step do you already do in Excel?

objects.text: Python: the describe method. Excel: AVERAGE, STDEV.S, MIN, QUARTILE, MEDIAN, MAX.

slides.notes:
The describe call gives eight summary numbers for a numeric variable, and here they are for the order value. The mean is 47,491 shillings and the median, the middle order, is 23,200. The mean is 2.0 times the median. That gap is the sign of a right-skewed distribution: a few very large orders pull the mean up.

The largest order is 3,104,000 shillings. The standard deviation of 123,574 is bigger than the mean, which tells you the values are spread widely. Quartile one and quartile three, 9,940 and 47,300, mark the middle half of the orders. So which would you quote as the typical order, the mean or the median?

title.text:
Step 3, one variable: a histogram
shows the shape of the distribution

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_f_panels_7.70x4.80_8cae1f76.png
objects.alt: Step 3, one variable: a histogram shows the shape of the distribution

objects.text: A histogram counts how many records fall in each bin (a range of values).

runs.text: Tall bars on the left: most orders are small.
Long right tail: the mean 47,491 is right of the median 23,200.
720 orders above 200,000 are off the chart.

slides.notes:
This is a histogram. It splits the order value into bins, each ten thousand shillings wide, and the height of a bar counts the orders in that bin. The picture is drawn with seaborn histplot. Most orders are small, so the tall bars sit on the left. The gold line is the median and the dashed red line is the mean.

The mean sits to the right because of the long tail, which is the right skew. The chart stops at two hundred thousand shillings for readability. 720 orders, 2.4 percent, are larger and are off the chart, and the largest is 3,104,000. Why would a bar chart of the average hide this shape?

title.text: matplotlib draws on a Figure that holds an Axes

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_f_anatomy_11.90x4.25_1cd90a14.png
objects.alt: matplotlib draws on a Figure that holds an Axes

objects.text: An axis is one scale. The Axes holds both.

slides.notes:
matplotlib is the drawing library under almost every Python chart, and it has two objects to know. The Figure is the whole page. The Axes is the plot area on that page, with its scales, the line or bars, and their labels. One call, plt dot subplots, gives you both, and the convention is to name them fig and ax.

Then you draw on ax and label it: a title, a y label, an x label. Be careful with the word. An axis is one scale, the x or the y. The Axes is the whole plot area that holds them. In Excel you would select a chart and add axis titles.

Here each is one line of code, so the chart can be rebuilt tomorrow with new data. Which number on the picture is the Axes?

ax.plot draws one line. set_title and set_ylabel add the words.
The last line checks the types: a Figure and an Axes. In Colab the chart appears under the cell.

Read this recipe before we use it in the lab. The first two lines total the order value for each month, in millions of shillings. Then plt dot subplots makes the Figure and the Axes. We draw one line on the Axes with ax dot plot, then label it with a title and a y label that says the units.

Without units nobody knows what the numbers mean. The final print confirms what we hold: a Figure and an Axes. When you run it in Colab, the chart appears under the cell. Why do we put the unit in the label?

slides.notes:
Before more code, a decision guide. Start from the question and the chart follows. One numeric variable, and you want its shape: a histogram. A numeric variable compared across groups: a box plot. Two numeric variables together: a scatter plot. Which group has the larger mean or count: a bar chart.

A number over time: a line chart. seaborn is a library built on matplotlib. You give it the DataFrame and the names of the columns, and it draws the chart and returns an Axes that you can still label. Its hue setting colours the marks by a categorical variable.

Which question in this table is closest to one you ask at work?

title.text:
A box plot compares the spread of
order value across payment methods

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_f_panels_7.70x4.80_3dac0d6e.png
objects.alt: A box plot compares the spread of order value across payment methods

objects.text: Each box holds the middle half of the orders, from Q1 to Q3. The line inside is the median.

runs.text: Whiskers end at the last order within 1.5 x IQR of the box.
About 2,100 orders (6.9%) are above the fence, 103,340 UGX.
Medians within 800 UGX. Each box fence is within 1,206 of it.

slides.notes:
A box plot shows the shape of a numeric variable for each group, side by side. The box runs from quartile one to quartile three, so it holds the middle half of the orders. The line inside the box is the median. The whiskers end at the last order that lies within one and a half times the interquartile range beyond the box.

Values beyond are outliers. About 2,100 orders, 6.9 percent, lie above the fence of 103,340 shillings, which is Q3 plus one and a half times the IQR for all orders. Each box has its own fence, within 1,206 shillings of that. We hide those orders with showfliers equals False.

The finding is that the three boxes are almost identical. The medians are 23,825, 23,025 and 23,280. Payment method does not change the typical order. Would you have guessed that?

title.text:
Step 4, two variables: a scatter plot
shows whether they move together

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_f_panels_7.70x4.80_72a04105.png
objects.alt: Step 4, two variables: a scatter plot shows whether they move together

objects.text: Bigger baskets cost more. The correlation is r = 0.30.

runs.text: r runs from -1 to 1. About 0.3 is modest.
hue colours points by payment method. No colour stands apart.
36 points above 300,000 are off the chart.

slides.notes:
A scatter plot puts one numeric variable on each axis, and every point is one record. Here are two thousand randomly chosen orders. Basket size, the number of lines on the order, runs along the bottom, and the order value up the side. The points rise to the right, so bigger baskets cost more.

The correlation coefficient, Pearson r, is 0.30. That is a modest link, because the price of the products varies a lot. The hue setting colours each point by payment method. The three colours are mixed, so payment method does not explain anything here. 36 points are above three hundred thousand and are off the chart.

Correlation is not causation. What else could drive both?

title.text:
A bar chart of means needs its error
bars: the branches barely differ

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_f_panels_7.70x4.80_fe2c8f92.png
objects.alt: A bar chart of means needs its error bars: the branches barely differ

objects.text: sns.barplot draws each group mean. The black line is a 95 percent confidence interval.

runs.text: The intervals overlap: the gap may be sampling variability. This is no test.

slides.notes:
Now a bar chart, drawn with seaborn barplot. By default it plots the mean of each group, and the black line on each bar is a confidence interval, a range that is built to catch the true mean about ninety five times in a hundred. The highest branch mean is B04, 49,618 shillings, and the lowest is B06, 44,374.

The bars look alike, and the lines overlap. When intervals overlap like this, it is a warning that the gap between the two branches may be sampling variability. Overlap is not a formal test, and here we also picked the highest and the lowest of eight branches. We do not claim a difference from these bars.

Next session we learn how to test it properly. Why does a bar chart without the error bars invite a wrong conclusion?

title.text:
Step 5, groups: B01 has the most
returns, but B07 has the highest rate

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_f_panels_11.90x4.25_881b21e3.png
objects.alt: Step 5, groups: B01 has the most returns, but B07 has the highest rate

objects.text: Red marks the top bar. B01 is Kampala Central. B07 is Fort Portal.

slides.notes:
Here is a result that fools almost everyone the first time. On the left, the count of returns. Branch B01, Kampala Central, has the most, 321. On the right, the rate, which is returns per hundred lines sold. Now the top bar is branch B07, Fort Portal, at 3.18.

The two charts name different branches. The count favours big branches, because a branch that sells more has more things to return. B01 sold 19,169 lines. The rate divides by what was sold, so branches of different size can be compared fairly. Which chart would you show to the manager who asks which branch has a returns problem?

title.text:
A rate divides the count by what could
have happened: returns per 100 lines sold

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x2.14_6ef39e3b.png
objects.alt: A rate divides the count by what could have happened: returns per 100 lines sold

rows.text: What could have happened: the lines sold.
Total returns over total lines, times 100.

objects.text: A rate is a ratio of events to opportunities. A percentage is a rate per 100.

slides.notes:
The rate is a short formula. Take the count of returns, divide by the lines sold, and multiply by one hundred. The lines sold are the denominator: everything that could have been returned. For branch B07, 293 returns divided by 9,227 lines, times one hundred, gives 3.18 returns per hundred lines.

Across all branches the rate is 2,056 returns over 98,066 lines, which is 2.10. So B07 returns about one and a half times as often as the whole company. In Excel this is a calculated column that divides one column by another. What would the denominator be for a complaint rate?

slides.notes:
Here are all eight branches with the count, the lines sold, the rate and the two rankings. Branch B01 ranks first by count and 8th, which is last, by rate. Branch B07 ranks 2nd by count and first by rate. The count told us about the size of the branch.

The rate tells us about behaviour. To build this table we joined the returns and the order lines to the orders, to get the branch, then counted each. That is the merge you practised in Session 9. When you see a ranking by count in a report, which question should you ask before you believe it?

title.text:
Seasonality: revenue peaked in December in
both years, because there were more orders

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_f_panels_11.90x4.25_2211c8e1.png
objects.alt: Seasonality: revenue peaked in December in both years, because there were more orders

objects.text: Each line is one year over the same twelve months. Both years rise in December.

slides.notes:
Now a line chart over time, with a trick. Instead of one long line, we draw each year as its own line over the same twelve months. That makes a repeating pattern easy to see. On the left is revenue. Both years climb in December, to 89.5 million in 2024 and 72.8 million in 2025.

On the right is the number of orders, which climbs in the same month. The December order count was 1,811 and 1,617. The average order value barely moved, 49,399 in December 2024 against 47,512 in the other months of both years. So the peak comes from more orders: the average order value stayed near 47,500.

What might bring more shoppers in December?

December revenue was 1.55 and 1.26
times the average of the other months

objects.alt: December revenue was 1.55 and 1.26 times the average of the other months

objects.text: A time series has a trend, seasonality and noise. This one has a clear seasonal peak.

runs.text: Trend: slow rise or fall. Seasonality: yearly repeat. Noise: random variation.
Mean of the 22 other months: 57.9 million.

slides.notes:
A time series, which is a number measured over time, is usually described by three parts. The trend is the slow movement up or down. The seasonality is the pattern that repeats each year. And the noise is the random variation that is left. Together they are called the decomposition.

Here the red bars are the two Decembers. The dashed line is the average of the other twenty two months, 57.9 million shillings. December 2024 was 1.55 times that and December 2025 was 1.26 times. The limit is important. We have only two Decembers, so we can say the pattern repeated once.

With more years we could say more. How many years of data would you want?

title.text:
Step 6, write: a finding states a
number, a comparison and a limit

objects.text: Weak

runs.text: Returns are high in Kampala Central.

objects.text: Strong

runs.text: Kampala Central has the most returns (321) but the lowest rate: 1.67 per 100 lines sold, against 2.10 overall.

objects.text: If you cannot write the sentence, you have not finished exploring.

slides.notes:
The last step of the routine is to write. A finding is one sentence with three parts. A number says how big the thing is. A comparison says against what. And a limit says what the data cannot tell us. The weak version says returns are high in Kampala Central.

A reader cannot check it. The strong version says Kampala Central has the most returns, 321, but the lowest rate, 1.67 per hundred lines sold, against 2.10 for all branches, and it names the limit: this is a sample of orders over two years. Which of your own reports would you rewrite this way?
